quote: 20.1 Vendor shall defend, indemnify, and hold harmless Customer, its Affiliates, and their directors, officers, employees, and agents from each third-party claim and resulting damages, settlements, judgments, penalties, costs, and reasonable attorneys' fees arising from an allegation that the Services or Deliverables infringe or misappropriate an intellectual property right.
rationale: The indemnity package meets the preferred position in full. § 20.1 gives an unqualified Vendor defence and indemnity for third-party IP infringement/misappropriation claims covering Customer, its Affiliates and their personnel; § 20.2 adds Vendor indemnities for breach of Applicable Law, bodily injury/property damage, unauthorized access to or disclosure of Customer Data caused by Vendor, and Vendor's gross negligence, wilful misconduct or fraud. § 20.4 sets out standard procedure (prompt notice with material-prejudice qualifier, cooperation at the indemnifying party's expense, control of defence, and settlement consent protections). Customer's reverse indemnity in § 20.3 stays narrow — limited to unmodified Customer-supplied material used strictly as authorized and Customer's own violation of Applicable Law, with express carve-outs for Vendor Technology, modification, combination or Vendor instructions. § 20.5 provides the usual infringement remedies (procure, modify/replace, or terminate and refund) as an addition to, not a substitute for, the defence obligation, and bars termination of unaffected Services. Indemnification obligations are also carved out of the liability cap as "Excluded Claims" under § 21.3, so the Vendor IP indemnity is not squeezed by the general cap and no 3× super-cap fallback is needed. Nothing here is one-sided against us; no redline required.

quote: 14.2 Upon creation and subject to payment of the applicable Fees, Customer owns each Deliverable created specifically for Customer. Vendor hereby assigns to Customer all worldwide right, title, and interest in those Deliverables and shall obtain equivalent assignments from its personnel.
rationale: Section 14 meets the preferred position in full. 14.1 confirms Customer owns all Customer Data, Customer Confidential Information and independently developed IP, with no transfer to Vendor beyond a limited processing right (reinforced by 15.1's no-sale/no-advertising/no-model-training restriction and 1.8's exclusion of Customer Data from Vendor Technology). 14.2 vests ownership of each Deliverable in Customer on creation with an express present assignment from Vendor plus personnel assignments and further-assurances. 14.3 lets Vendor retain only its pre-existing Vendor Technology and back-stops embedded Vendor Technology with the perpetual, irrevocable, worldwide, royalty-free, fully paid, modify-and-derivative licence in 13.2 (sublicensable to Affiliates and contractors under 13.1/13.3). 14.4 negates joint ownership absent a separate signed instrument setting exploitation rights, and feedback use is limited to generalized suggestions with Customer retaining unrestricted rights in its own feedback. Nothing assigns Customer IP or data to Vendor, so no walk-away trigger. Minor, non-material notes only: ownership in 14.2 is conditioned on payment of Fees; "Deliverable" (1.4) captures only work product an Order Form identifies as created specifically for Customer; 1.3 carves anonymized, non-linkable operational telemetry out of Customer Data; and 14.1's processing right extends to "improve the Services for Customer" (bounded by 15.1). None of these warrants a redline.
ruleTitle: Ownership of deliverables and Customer Data

quote: 21.1 Except for Excluded Claims, each Party's total aggregate liability arising out of or relating to this Agreement shall not exceed the greater of the Fees paid or payable by Customer during the twelve months preceding the event giving rise to the claim and USD 1,000,000. The cap is mutual and applies regardless of the form of action or number of claims.
rationale: Section 21 meets the preferred position in full. §21.1 sets a single mutual cap at the greater of (a) Fees paid or payable by Customer in the twelve months preceding the event and (b) USD 1,000,000, expressly stated to be mutual — no one-sided or uncapped Customer exposure. §21.2 is a mutual exclusion of indirect/consequential damages, with helpful carve-ins confirming data restoration, replacement services, notification and incident-response costs are direct damages. §21.3 defines "Excluded Claims" (uncapped) to cover breach of confidentiality, data-protection or security obligations, indemnification obligations, gross negligence, wilful misconduct or fraud, and infringement of the other Party's IP, and confirms Customer's obligation to pay undisputed Fees is not "damages" subject to the cap. "Fees" (§1.5) is a substantive recurring/subscription/services fee base, so the cap is not illusory, and §18.2 confirms insurance does not limit Vendor's liabilities. No competing or hidden aggregate-liability language appears elsewhere in the document. No redline needed.
ruleTitle: Limitation of liability — cap, mutuality and carve-outs

quote: 24.1 Customer may assign this Agreement or an Order Form without Vendor's consent to an Affiliate or to a successor in a merger, reorganization, acquisition, or sale of all or substantially all assets or business to which the Agreement relates.
rationale: Section 24 meets the preferred position on every material term. 24.1 gives us consent-free assignment to an Affiliate or to a successor in a merger, reorganization, acquisition or sale of substantially all assets (subject only to prompt notice and assignee assumption, which is acceptable). 24.2 binds Vendor asymmetrically in our favour: no assignment, delegation of material performance, or transfer by change of control without our prior written consent (reasonableness qualified only as to capable, financially sound assignees), and never to a direct Customer competitor without our consent. 24.3 leaves a mutual not-unreasonably-withheld standard for residual assignments. 24.4 expressly denies Vendor any right to terminate, suspend, reprice, accelerate Fees or reduce service on our change of control, and requires cooperation with administrative changes for a permitted successor — squarely avoiding walk-away territory. 13.3 aligns the licence transfer right with a Section 24 permitted assignment. A document-wide search confirms no other change-of-control trigger; 9.2 is an insolvency clause and expressly states a lawful reorganization is not by itself grounds for termination. No redline needed.

proposal.comment: [Playbook] We have deleted the sole-and-exclusive-provider commitment in Section 2.2: our playbook does not permit exclusivity or sole-supplier obligations on Customer, and this clause also contradicts Sections 2.1 (no purchase commitment) and 12.3 (Vendor's acknowledgement that Customer has made no exclusivity commitment). If Vendor needs some volume protection, we could consider exclusivity limited to a defined product category for no more than 12 months, ending automatically if Vendor misses service levels or delivery dates.

quote: 2.2 Vendor will be Customer's sole and exclusive provider of hosted analytics services throughout the term.
rationale: Section 2.2 binds Customer to Vendor as its sole and exclusive provider of hosted analytics services for the entire term. This is exclusive dealing for the full term with no performance-based exit — walk-away territory under the rule, and it fails the fallback (which requires a defined category, a 12-month limit, and automatic termination on Vendor's service-level or delivery failure). It also directly conflicts with Section 2.1 (no minimum quantity or purchase commitment) and Section 12.3 (Vendor acknowledges Customer has made no exclusivity commitment), so deletion of Section 2.2 is the smallest edit that reaches the preferred position and resolves the internal inconsistency. No other exclusivity provision binds Customer; the remaining "exclusive" references (licence grant, remedies, jurisdiction) are unrelated.

Instead, Vendor receives an equitable extension of affected timelines, which addresses the underlying delay risk.

ops.newText: If Customer delays in providing a dependency, Vendor's sole and exclusive remedy shall be an equitable extension of the affected timelines. No liquidated damages, penalty or similar payment shall be payable by Customer under this Agreement.

quote: 7.6 Customer shall pay Vendor USD 25,000 per day as agreed liquidated damages for any delay in providing a dependency.
rationale: Section 7.6 imposes liquidated damages of USD 25,000 per day on us for "any delay in providing a dependency" — a Customer-payable penalty with no materiality threshold, no grace period and no aggregate cap, triggered by minor breaches. This fails both the preferred position (no liquidated damages or penalties payable by Customer) and the fallback (a single early-termination fee capped at 3 months' fees), and the "any delay" trigger plus unbounded daily accrual sits in walk-away territory. The mutual cap in § 21.1 does not cure it: it caps aggregate liability but leaves the LD mechanic intact and could still expose us to the greater of 12 months' Fees or USD 1,000,000, and the § 7.3 dispute-withholding right addresses invoiced amounts, not the penalty itself. No other Customer-payable LD or termination penalty appears in the document. Redline deletes the daily LD and gives Vendor schedule relief instead.

quote: 13.1 Subject to payment of applicable Fees, Vendor grants Customer, its Affiliates, and contractors acting on their behalf a worldwide, non-exclusive right during the subscription term to access and use the hosted Services and documentation for their internal business purposes and to provide services to Customer.
rationale: Section 13 meets the preferred position in full. 13.1 extends the subscription grant to Customer's Affiliates and to contractors acting on their behalf (and to Authorized Users), with no "non-transferable" or "revocable" qualifier. 13.2 gives Customer and its Affiliates a perpetual, irrevocable, worldwide, royalty-free, fully paid licence to delivered/embedded Vendor Technology, including modification and contractor support, and 14.3 confirms that licence reaches Vendor Technology needed to use a Deliverable. 13.3 bars any revocation or suspension except for a material uncured payment or use breach after notice and a reasonable cure opportunity — so there is no at-will revocation — and expressly permits transfer of licence rights to an Affiliate or successor in an assignment permitted by Section 24, which allows Customer to assign to an M&A successor without consent. 13.4's use restrictions are narrow (reverse engineering, interference, security bypass, unlawful use) and expressly do not limit authorized security testing or use of Customer Data and output, so they do not undercut the permitted use. No redline required.

quote: Nothing restricts Customer from developing, acquiring, licensing, selling, or using any product or service, engaging any supplier, hiring any person who responds to general recruitment, or conducting business in any field or territory. Vendor acknowledges that Customer has made no exclusivity, non-compete, most-favoured-customer, minimum-volume, or no-hire commitment.
rationale: Section 12.3 affirmatively preserves our freedom to develop, acquire, license, sell or use any product or service, engage any supplier, and operate in any field or territory, and confirms we have given no non-compete commitment. This meets the preferred position (no non-compete or field-of-use restriction on Customer) and benefits us. A full-text scan for "compet", field-of-use and "Customer shall not" language found no restriction binding us: the only competition reference (§ 24.2) restricts Vendor's assignment to our competitors, and § 13.4 is a standard acceptable-use limit on the Services rather than a field-of-use restriction on our business. The "sole and exclusive provider" language in § 2.2 is an exclusivity commitment addressed under the EXCLUSIVITY rule and is not double-flagged here; § 12.4's post-term non-solicit is likewise a no-hire issue outside this rule.

ops.text: Customer may terminate this Agreement or any Order Form for convenience, in whole or in part, upon thirty (30) days' prior written notice to Vendor, without penalty or early-termination fee, in which case Vendor shall refund any prepaid Fees for the period after the effective date of termination. quote: 9.3 Customer may terminate an Order Form immediately if Vendor suffers a material Security Incident, repeatedly misses a critical service level, violates Applicable Law in performing the Services, or infringes a third party's intellectual property and cannot provide the remedies required by Section 20.5.
rationale: Section 9 provides only for-cause (9.1), insolvency (9.2), security/service-failure (9.3) and Order-Form-scope (9.5) termination rights; Sections 6.2, 19.4, 20.5 and 27.3 are likewise all cause- or event-based. No termination-for-convenience right exists for either Party, and Section 8.1 fixes a three-year term with Order Forms auto-renewing on 180 days' notice under 8.2. Absence of any Customer convenience right in a multi-year term is walk-away territory under the rule, so this fails the fallback as a missing behaviour. Favourably, Vendor also has no convenience right, so our redline adds only a Customer-side 30-day right with a pro-rata refund of prepaid Fees (supported by the existing refund mechanic in 10.2) and confirms Vendor has none.

proposal.comment: [Playbook] We can accommodate usage verification, but not unlimited, unannounced audits with remote access to our systems: our position is one audit per 12 months on 30 days' written notice, during business hours, by an independent auditor bound by confidentiality, and no access to our systems (consistent with Section 22.2). If helpful, we can accept 15 days' notice as a fallback.

The audit will be conducted through records and reports Customer provides, and Vendor and its auditor have no right to access Customer's systems remotely or otherwise.

proposal.summary: Limit Vendor audits to once per 12 months on 30 days' notice, during business hours, by an independent auditor bound by confidentiality, with no access to our systems.

quote: 22.1 Vendor may audit Customer at any time without notice and may remotely access Customer's systems and records for that purpose.
rationale: Section 22.1 gives Vendor unlimited, unannounced audit rights plus remote access to our systems — squarely in walk-away territory and failing the fallback on frequency, notice and system access. Sections 22.2 and 22.3 already meet the preferred position on cost allocation (Vendor bears cost unless underpayment exceeds 5%), no direct system or unrelated data access, and confidentiality of findings, so the minimal fix is to rewrite 22.1 to add once-per-12-months frequency, 30 days' written notice, business-hours conduct, an independent confidentiality-bound auditor, and deletion of the remote-access language.

quote: 28.1 This Agreement and each dispute arising from it are governed by the laws of the State of New York, without regard to conflict-of-law principles. The United Nations Convention on Contracts for the International Sale of Goods does not apply.
rationale: Section 28.1 selects New York law (with CISG disapplied) and Section 28.2 confers exclusive jurisdiction on the state and federal courts in New York County, with mutual submission to personal jurisdiction and waiver of venue objections — exactly the preferred position. There is no arbitration provision anywhere in the document, so no foreign seat concern. Section 28.3's fifteen-business-day executive escalation is a mutual pre-filing step that expressly does not delay urgent relief or limitations-preserving filings, and Section 28.2 preserves interim injunctive relief in other courts; neither undercuts the accepted law/forum selection. No redline needed.

If some price assurance is important, we could discuss a narrow MFN limited to a defined product for 12 months with reasonable-comparison carve-outs.

quote: 7.2 Customer shall offer Vendor terms no less favourable than the best terms Customer offers any other technology supplier.
rationale: Section 7.2 imposes an MFN running against us: we would have to give Vendor terms no less favourable than the best terms offered to any other technology supplier. It is unlimited in scope, product and duration and has no comparison carve-outs, so it fails the fallback (defined product, 12 months, reasonable-comparison carve-outs) and sits in walk-away territory (open-ended obligation to extend better third-party terms). It also contradicts Section 12.3, where Vendor acknowledges we have made no most-favoured-customer commitment. No Vendor-granted MFN in our favour exists to preserve, so the minimal fix is deletion of the obligation.

rationale: The Agreement meets the preferred position: § 2.1 expressly disclaims any minimum quantity or purchase commitment, limits our payment obligation to Services actually ordered under an executed Order Form, and confirms that declining to place further orders is neither a breach nor a shortfall. § 12.3 reinforces this with Vendor's acknowledgement that we have made no minimum-volume (or exclusivity/MFC/no-hire) commitment, and § 7.1 bars Vendor from imposing any minimum-use or similar charge not identified in the Order Form. The only "shortfall" references (§§ 22.2–22.3) relate to audited underpayment for actual usage, not a take-or-pay commitment, and no volume caps on our usage appear. No redline needed.

We cannot accept a no-hire ("or engage") covering everyone employed by Vendor at any time during the term, which also conflicts with the general-recruitment freedom preserved in Section 12.3.

ops.newText: 12.4 For twelve months after the end of a person's involvement in the Services, neither party will knowingly solicit for employment any employee of the other party who was directly involved in performing or receiving the Services. This Section 12.4 does not restrict either party from (a) placing or responding to general advertisements or recruitment campaigns not specifically targeted at the other party's personnel, or (b) hiring or engaging any person who approaches it on an unsolicited basis or who responds to such general advertising or recruitment, and neither party is subject to any no-hire obligation.

proposal.summary: Narrow one-sided 18-month no-hire to a mutual 12-month non-solicit limited to personnel involved in the services, with general-advertising and unsolicited-approach carve-outs

quote: 12.4 For eighteen months after termination Customer will not solicit or engage any person employed by Vendor at any time during the term.
rationale: Section 12.4 binds only the Customer and fails the fallback on every material term: it is one-sided rather than mutual, runs eighteen months rather than twelve, covers any person employed by Vendor at any time during the term rather than only personnel directly involved in the Services, contains no general-advertising or unsolicited-approach carve-out, and — by barring Customer from "engaging" such persons — is an outright no-hire, which is walk-away territory under the rule. It also conflicts with Section 12.3, where Vendor acknowledges Customer has made no no-hire commitment and is free to hire anyone responding to general recruitment. Because the parties have evidently bargained for some restriction, we narrow to the fallback (mutual, 12 months from the end of involvement, services personnel only, with advertising and unsolicited-approach carve-outs and no no-hire) rather than deleting the clause outright.

We propose shortening the window to 30 days and adding a 60-day Vendor renewal reminder to reach the preferred position; a window of up to 60 days would be an acceptable fallback.

quote: 11.1 Upon expiry or termination for any reason, Vendor shall, at Customer's request, provide reasonable transition assistance for up to six months at the rates in the expiring Order Form. Assistance includes knowledge transfer, export support, cooperation with a replacement supplier, orderly migration, and continued service at the then-current scope and service levels.
rationale: Section 11 meets the preferred position in full: 11.1 gives up to six months of transition assistance on termination for any reason at the expiring Order Form rates (rates no higher than then-current, which favours us), including knowledge transfer, migration and cooperation with a replacement supplier; 11.2 requires return of all Customer Data within thirty days in a complete, commonly used, documented machine-readable format with metadata, and bars withholding data over a fee dispute; and 11.3 requires secure deletion after confirmed return with written certification by an authorized officer, with any law-required retained copy remaining protected. Section 16.5 expressly defers Customer Data to Sections 11 and 15, and Sections 10.1–10.2 preserve access through the transition period and Deliverable/refund rights, so there is no conflicting immediate-deletion or data-hostage term. Deletion is keyed to Customer's confirmation of successful return rather than a fixed 30-day trigger, which is a timing nuance in our favour and not a deviation.
